Paragraph: This is especially evident in weak type 1 inflammation-inducing viruses such as RV and RSV (Kling et al., 2005; Wood et al., 2011; Ravi et al., 2019) . Additionally, there are also evidence of reduced type I (IFNβ) and III (IFNλ) interferon production due to type 2-skewed inflammation, which contributes to imperfect clearance of the virus resulting in persistence of viral components, or the live virus in the airway epithelium (Contoli et al., 2006; Hwang et al., 2019; Wark, 2019) . Due to the viral components remaining in the airway, antiviral genes such as type I interferons, inflammasome activating factors and cytokines remained activated resulting in prolong airway inflammation (Wood et al., 2011; Essaidi-Laziosi et al., 2018) . These factors enhance granulocyte infiltration thus prolonging the exacerbation symptoms. Such persistent inflammation may also be found within DNA viruses such as AdV, hCMV and HSV, whose infections generally persist longer (Imperiale and Jiang, 2015) , further contributing to chronic activation of inflammation when they infect the airway (Yang et al., 2008; Morimoto et al., 2009; Imperiale and Jiang, 2015; Lan et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2016; Kowalski et al., 2017) . With that note, human papilloma virus (HPV), a DNA virus highly associated with head and neck cancers and respiratory papillomatosis, is also linked with the chronic inflammation that precedes the malignancies (de Visser et al., 2005; Gillison et al., 2012; Bonomi et al., 2014; Fernandes et al., 2015) . Therefore, the role of HPV infection in causing chronic inflammation in the airway and their association to exacerbations of chronic airway inflammatory diseases, which is scarcely explored, should be investigated in the future. Furthermore, viral persistence which lead to continuous expression of antiviral genes may also lead to the development of steroid resistance, which is seen with RV, RSV, and PIV infection (Chi et al., 2011; Ford et al., 2013; Papi et al., 2013) . The use of steroid to suppress the inflammation may also cause the virus to linger longer in the airway due to the lack of antiviral clearance (Kim et al., 2008; Hammond et al., 2015; Hewitt et al., 2016; McKendry et al., 2016; Singanayagam et al., 2019b) . The concomitant development of steroid resistance together with recurring or prolong viral infection thus added considerable burden to the management of acute exacerbation, which should be the future focus of research to resolve the dual complications arising from viral infection. On the other end of the spectrum, viruses that induce strong type 1 inflammation and cell death such as IFV (Yan et al., 2016; Guibas et al., 2018) and certain CoV (including the recently emerged COVID-19 virus) (Tao et al., 2013; Yue et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) , may not cause prolonged inflammation due to strong induction of antiviral clearance. These infections, however, cause massive damage and cell death to the epithelial barrier, so much so that areas of the epithelium may be completely absent post infection (Yan et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2019) . Factors such as RANTES and CXCL10, which recruit immune cells to induce apoptosis, are strongly induced from IFV infected epithelium (Ampomah et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2019) . Additionally, necroptotic factors such as RIP3 further compounds the cell deaths in IFV infected epithelium . The massive cell death induced may result in worsening of the acute exacerbation due to the release of their cellular content into the airway, further evoking an inflammatory response in the airway (Guibas et al., 2018) . Moreover, the destruction of the epithelial barrier may cause further contact with other pathogens and allergens in the airway which may then prolong exacerbations or results in new exacerbations. Epithelial destruction may also promote further epithelial remodeling during its regeneration as viral infection induces the expression of remodeling genes such as MMPs and growth factors . Infections that cause massive destruction of the epithelium, such as IFV, usually result in severe acute exacerbations with non-classical symptoms of chronic airway inflammatory diseases. Fortunately, annual vaccines are available to prevent IFV infections (Vasileiou et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018) ; and it is recommended that patients with chronic airway inflammatory disease receive their annual influenza vaccination as the best means to prevent severe IFV induced exacerbation. 

Another mechanism that viral infections may use to drive acute exacerbations is the induction of vasodilation or tight junction opening factors which may increase the rate of infiltration. Infection with a multitude of respiratory viruses causes disruption of tight junctions with the resulting increased rate of viral infiltration. This also increases the chances of allergens coming into contact with airway immune cells. For example, IFV infection was found to induce oncostatin M (OSM) which causes tight junction opening (Pothoven et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2018) . Similarly, RV and RSV infections usually cause tight junction opening which may also increase the infiltration rate of eosinophils and thus worsening of the classical symptoms of chronic airway inflammatory diseases (Sajjan et al., 2008; Kast et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018) . In addition, the expression of vasodilating factors and fluid homeostatic factors such as angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) and bactericidal/permeabilityincreasing fold-containing family member A1 (BPIFA1) are also associated with viral infections and pneumonia development, which may worsen inflammation in the lower airway Akram et al., 2018) . These factors may serve as targets to prevent viral-induced exacerbations during the management of acute exacerbation of chronic airway inflammatory diseases. Another recent area of interest is the relationship between asthma and COPD exacerbations and their association with the airway microbiome. The development of chronic airway inflammatory diseases is usually linked to specific bacterial species in the microbiome which may thrive in the inflamed airway environment (Diver et al., 2019) . In the event of a viral infection such as RV infection, the effect induced by the virus may destabilize the equilibrium of the microbiome present (Molyneaux et al., 2013; Kloepfer et al., 2014; Kloepfer et al., 2017; Jubinville et al., 2018; van Rijn et al., 2019) . In addition, viral infection may disrupt biofilm colonies in the upper airway (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae) microbiome to be release into the lower airway and worsening the inflammation (Marks et al., 2013; Chao et al., 2014) . Moreover, a viral infection may also alter the nutrient profile in the airway through release of previously inaccessible nutrients that will alter bacterial growth (Siegel et al., 2014; Mallia et al., 2018) . Furthermore, the destabilization is further compounded by impaired bacterial immune response, either from direct viral influences, or use of corticosteroids to suppress the exacerbation symptoms (Singanayagam et al., 2018 (Singanayagam et al., , 2019a Wang et al., 2018; Finney et al., 2019) . All these may gradually lead to more far reaching effect when normal flora is replaced with opportunistic pathogens, altering the inflammatory profiles (Teo et al., 2018) . These changes may in turn result in more severe and frequent acute exacerbations due to the interplay between virus and pathogenic bacteria in exacerbating chronic airway inflammatory diseases (Wark et al., 2013; Singanayagam et al., 2018) . To counteract these effects, microbiome-based therapies are in their infancy but have shown efficacy in the treatments of irritable bowel syndrome by restoring the intestinal microbiome (Bakken et al., 2011) . Further research can be done similarly for the airway microbiome to be able to restore the microbiome following disruption by a viral infection. Viral infections can cause the disruption of mucociliary function, an important component of the epithelial barrier. Ciliary proteins FIGURE 2 | Changes in the upper airway epithelium contributing to viral exacerbation in chronic airway inflammatory diseases. The upper airway epithelium is the primary contact/infection site of most respiratory viruses. Therefore, its infection by respiratory viruses may have far reaching consequences in augmenting and synergizing current and future acute exacerbations. The destruction of epithelial barrier, mucociliary function and cell death of the epithelial cells serves to increase contact between environmental triggers with the lower airway and resident immune cells. The opening of tight junction increasing the leakiness further augments the inflammation and exacerbations. In addition, viral infections are usually accompanied with oxidative stress which will further increase the local inflammation in the airway. The dysregulation of inflammation can be further compounded by modulation of miRNAs and epigenetic modification such as DNA methylation and histone modifications that promote dysregulation in inflammation. Finally, the change in the local airway environment and inflammation promotes growth of pathogenic bacteria that may replace the airway microbiome. Furthermore, the inflammatory environment may also disperse upper airway commensals into the lower airway, further causing inflammation and alteration of the lower airway environment, resulting in prolong exacerbation episodes following viral infection. As RV, RSV, and IFV were the most frequently studied viruses in chronic airway inflammatory diseases, most of the viruses listed are predominantly these viruses. However, the mechanisms stated here may also be applicable to other viruses but may not be listed as they were not implicated in the context of chronic airway inflammatory diseases exacerbation (see text for abbreviations). that aid in the proper function of the motile cilia in the airways are aberrantly expressed in ciliated airway epithelial cells which are the major target for RV infection (Griggs et al., 2017) . Such form of secondary cilia dyskinesia appears to be present with chronic inflammations in the airway, but the exact mechanisms are still unknown (Peng et al., , 2019 Qiu et al., 2018) . Nevertheless, it was found that in viral infection such as IFV, there can be a change in the metabolism of the cells as well as alteration in the ciliary gene expression, mostly in the form of down-regulation of the genes such as dynein axonemal heavy chain 5 (DNAH5) and multiciliate differentiation And DNA synthesis associated cell cycle protein (MCIDAS) (Tan et al., 2018b . The recently emerged Wuhan CoV was also found to reduce ciliary beating in infected airway epithelial cell model (Zhu et al., 2020) . Furthermore, viral infections such as RSV was shown to directly destroy the cilia of the ciliated cells and almost all respiratory viruses infect the ciliated cells (Jumat et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2018a) . In addition, mucus overproduction may also disrupt the equilibrium of the mucociliary function following viral infection, resulting in symptoms of acute exacerbation (Zhu et al., 2009) . Hence, the disruption of the ciliary movement during viral infection may cause more foreign material and allergen to enter the airway, aggravating the symptoms of acute exacerbation and making it more difficult to manage. The mechanism of the occurrence of secondary cilia dyskinesia can also therefore be explored as a means to limit the effects of viral induced acute exacerbation. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short non-coding RNAs involved in post-transcriptional modulation of biological processes, and implicated in a number of diseases (Tan et al., 2014) . miRNAs are found to be induced by viral infections and may play a role in the modulation of antiviral responses and inflammation (Gutierrez et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018) . In the case of chronic airway inflammatory diseases, circulating miRNA changes were found to be linked to exacerbation of the diseases (Wardzynska et al., 2020) . Therefore, it is likely that such miRNA changes originated from the infected epithelium and responding immune cells, which may serve to further dysregulate airway inflammation leading to exacerbations. Both IFV and RSV infections has been shown to increase miR-21 and augmented inflammation in experimental murine asthma models, which is reversed with a combination treatment of anti-miR-21 and corticosteroids (Kim et al., 2017) . IFV infection is also shown to increase miR-125a and b, and miR-132 in COPD epithelium which inhibits A20 and MAVS; and p300 and IRF3, respectively, resulting in increased susceptibility to viral infections (Hsu et al., 2016 (Hsu et al., , 2017 . Conversely, miR-22 was shown to be suppressed in asthmatic epithelium in IFV infection which lead to aberrant epithelial response, contributing to exacerbations (Moheimani et al., 2018) . Other than these direct evidence of miRNA changes in contributing to exacerbations, an increased number of miRNAs and other non-coding RNAs responsible for immune modulation are found to be altered following viral infections (Globinska et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2018; Hasegawa et al., 2018) .

Question: What is recommended that patients with chronic airway inflammatory disease?
patients with chronic airway inflammatory disease receive their annual influenza vaccination as the best means to prevent severe IFV induced exacerbation.

1. Topic Description and Justification (300 words)
The COVID-19 pandemic has affected the economic, social, and psychological well-being of people globally. In Africa, the pandemic has had a significant impact on consumer behavior in terms of purchasing patterns, preferences, and attitudes towards brands. This study seeks to investigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on African consumer behavior.

The study is worthy of attention because it provides insights into the current trends, patterns, and preferences of African consumers during a crisis. The study will enable policymakers, marketers, and businesses to understand the evolving consumer behavior and tailor their strategies to meet the changing needs of consumers. Additionally, the pandemic has highlighted the importance of the role of technology in facilitating the purchasing habits of consumers.

2. Research Aim and Objectives (200 words)
The primary aim of this study is to investigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on African consumer behavior. The objectives of the study include:

- To examine the changes in consumer behavior that have resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic
- To identify the key factors influencing African consumer behavior during the pandemic
- To evaluate the role of technology in facilitating consumer behavior during the pandemic
- To recommend strategies that businesses can adopt to meet the changing needs of African consumers during the pandemic

3. Literature Review (700 words)
The literature review will explore the theories and concepts related to consumer behavior during crises, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on consumer behavior globally, and the role of technology in consumer behavior.

4. Conceptual Framework (500 words)
The conceptual framework will illustrate the potential areas of study and how the identified theorists have contributed to the development of the framework. The framework will include the key factors influencing African consumer behavior during the pandemic, including psychological, social, and economic factors, and the role of technology in facilitating consumer behavior.

5. Research Design and Methodology (200 words)
This study will use a quantitative research design and methodology. The study will use a survey to collect data from participants. The survey will be developed based on the identified research objectives and literature review.

6. Data Collection Method (200 words)
The survey will be administered online through email and social media platforms to reach a wide range of African consumers. The survey will have closed-ended questions and will be designed to gather data on changes in consumer behavior, the key factors influencing behavior, and the role of technology in facilitating behavior.

7. Data Analysis Approach (200 words)

8. Research Steps and Timescale (300 words)

The literature review will take three weeks, the survey design and administration will take four weeks, data analysis will take three weeks, and report writing will take two weeks. The final completion date is 12 weeks after the start of the study.

9. Ethical Considerations (300 words)
a) Participants will be informed about the nature and purpose of the research and how the data will be used through an informed consent form attached to the survey.
b) Participants will be required to give their consent to participate in the study by clicking on the informed consent form on the survey.
c) Participants can withdraw themselves and their data from the study at any time before the final report is written.

e) Data will be stored only on UWE computers with strong passwords, and access will be restricted to the research team.
f) Participants will be informed that their data will be kept for three years and will be destroyed after that.

The conceptual framework for this research proposal will illustrate the potential areas of study and how identified theorists have contributed to the development of the framework. The framework will include the key factors influencing African consumer behavior during the pandemic, including psychological, social, and economic factors, and the role of technology in facilitating consumer behavior.

Consumer behavior is affected by a combination of psychological, social, and economic factors. According to Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, human needs are arranged in a hierarchy, with physiological needs being the most basic and self-actualization needs being the highest. During the pandemic, physiological needs such as food, shelter, and personal protection become the most critical for survival. Therefore, the study will explore how consumers prioritize their consumption decisions during the pandemic, giving priority to their physiological needs.

Social factors such as social distancing protocols, isolation, and travel restrictions have compelled consumers to reduce their physical interactions, making them rely more on digital channels to meet their needs. This shift has enabled businesses and marketers to embrace online channels such as social media platforms for their marketing campaigns to reach their customers. The study will explore the impact of social factors on African consumer behavior during the pandemic, particularly how social distancing has led to dynamic changes in consumer preference.

Economic factors, such as unemployment and loss of income, have also had a significant impact on African consumer behavior during the pandemic. Many African consumers are facing financial hardships due to the pandemic and, as a result, are adjusting their consumption habits. The study will examine the impact of the pandemic on the buying power of African consumers and how their purchasing patterns have changed.

The theory of planned behavior (TPB) posits that consumer behavior is influenced by the attitude towards a specific product or service, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. TPB can explain why African consumers might make specific purchasing decisions during the pandemic, such as stockpiling and panic buying. It highlights the critical role of consumer attitude towards purchasing decisions during the pandemic and the role of subjective norms as well in influencing these decisions.

The conceptual framework also recognizes that technology has had an important role to play in facilitating consumer behavior during the pandemic. Consumers have managed to adapt and readapt to technological advancements and innovations, which has enabled them to continue their consumption habits during a challenging period. The framework acknowledges the importance of digital innovation in facilitating consumer behavior, such as online shopping, video conferencing, and digital payment methods, during the pandemic.

In conclusion, the conceptual framework for this research proposal identifies the key factors influencing African consumer behavior during the pandemic. Through exploring Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, the theory of planned behavior, and acknowledging the importance of technology, the framework is expected to provide insights into the evolving consumer behavior patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic in Africa. The carbon-halogen bond in an alkyl halide is polar and is cleaved on attack by a nucleophile so that the two electrons in the bond are retained by the halogen. Notice that all the examples in Table 8.1 involve alkyl halides, that is, compounds in which the halogen is attached to an sp³-hybridized carbon. Alkenyl halides and aryl halides, compounds in which the halogen is attached to sp²-hybridized carbons, are essentially unreactive under these conditions.

What types of carbon atoms are involved in alkyl halides, alkenyl halides, and aryl halides?

In alkyl halides, the carbon atom involved is sp³-hybridized. This means that the carbon atom in alkyl halides forms four single bonds, arranging its electrons into four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, which are oriented towards the corners of a tetrahedron.

In alkenyl halides, the carbon atom involved is sp²-hybridized. This type of carbon forms three bonds and has one π (pi) bond, leading to a trigonal planar geometry around the carbon atom. The sp² hybridization involves mixing one 's' orbital with two 'p' orbitals, leading to three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals and one remaining p orbital that is perpendicular to the plane formed by the hybrid orbitals.

In aryl halides, the carbon atom involved is also sp²-hybridized, similar to alkenyl halides. However, in aryl halides, the carbon atom is part of a benzene ring (or an aromatic system), which means that the sp²-hybridized carbons are part of a planar, six-membered ring. Each carbon in the ring is sp²-hybridized, with three σ bonds (one to each of its two neighboring carbons and one to a hydrogen atom) and participates in a delocalized π system above and below the plane of the ring, contributing to the aromaticity of the molecule.

The sp³ hybridization in alkyl halides makes the carbon-halogen bond more susceptible to nucleophilic attack compared to sp²-hybridized carbons in alkenyl and aryl halides. This is because the electron density around the sp³-hybridized carbon is more concentrated and accessible, which facilitates the formation of a new bond with the nucleophile, while the electrons in the carbon-halogen bond are retained by the more electronegative halogen. In contrast, the sp² hybridization in alkenyl and aryl halides leads to a more delocalized electron distribution, making the carbon less reactive towards nucleophilic attack under the conditions that are effective for alkyl halides.

You are given an array a of n integers.
You may permute (re-order) the elements arbitrarily. After the permutation is applied, compare the new array with the original one element by element. A position i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) is said to be "good" if the value that now stands at position i is strictly greater than the value that originally stood there.
Your task is to output the maximum possible number of good positions.

Input
The first line contains a single integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 100 000) — the length of the array.
The second line contains n integers a₁, a₂, …, aₙ (1 ≤ aᵢ ≤ 10⁹) — the elements of the array.

Output
Print one integer — the maximum possible number of positions whose new value is larger than the original value occupying that position.

Example
Input
7
10 1 1 1 5 5 3
Output
4

Example
Input
5
1 1 1 1 1
Output
0

To solve this problem, we need to **maximize the number of "good" positions** after permuting the array. A position `i` is good if the new value at position `i` is **strictly greater** than the original value at position `i`.

---

### Key Insight:
We can **sort the original array** and the **permutation**, and then try to **match elements** in a way that **maximizes the number of positions where the new value is greater** than the original.

Here's a step-by-step approach:

---

### Strategy:

1. **Sort the original array** `a` to get `a_sorted`.
2. **Sort a copy of the array** `b = a.copy()` to get `b_sorted`.
3. Now, we want to **match elements** from `b_sorted` to `a_sorted` such that as many elements in the new array are **strictly greater** than the original ones.

   - We use a **two-pointer approach**:
     - Initialize two pointers: `i` for `a_sorted`, and `j` for `b_sorted`.
     - For each element in `a_sorted`, try to find the **smallest element in `b_sorted`** that is **strictly greater** than it.
     - If found, increment both pointers and count it as a "good" position.
     - If not found, move to the next element in `a_sorted`.

---

### Why this works:

- By sorting both arrays, we can efficiently match the smallest possible larger element from the permutation to each element in the original array.
- This greedy strategy ensures we use the smallest possible values in the permutation to maximize the number of good positions.

---

### Python Code:

```python
def max_good_positions(n, a):
    a_sorted = sorted(a)
    b_sorted = sorted(a)
    
    i = j = good = 0
    while i < n and j < n:
        if b_sorted[j] > a_sorted[i]:
            good += 1
            i += 1
            j += 1
        else:
            j += 1
    return good

# Example usage
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
print(max_good_positions(n, a))
```

---

### Example Walkthrough:

**Input:**
```
7
10 1 1 1 5 5 3
```

**Sorted a = [1, 1, 1, 3, 5, 5, 10]**

Now, try to match each element with the smallest possible element in `b_sorted` that is **strictly greater**.

You can match:
- 1 → 1 (no)
- 1 → 1 (no)
- 1 → 1 (no)
- 3 → 5 (yes)
- 5 → 5 (no)
- 5 → 10 (yes)
- 10 → nothing (no)

Total good positions: **4**

---

### Time Complexity:
- Sorting: `O(n log n)`
- Two-pointer pass: `O(n)`
- **Overall: O(n log n)**

---

This is efficient and works for `n` up to 100,000.

---

### **1. Forest of Roots: Solving the Polynomial Equation**

Amelia encounters the polynomial:

$$
x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = 0
$$

This is a **cubic equation**, and to find the roots, we can attempt **factoring** or use the **Rational Root Theorem** to test possible rational roots.

#### **Step 1: Try Rational Root Theorem**

The Rational Root Theorem tells us that any rational root of the polynomial must be a factor of the **constant term** (−6) divided by a factor of the **leading coefficient** (1). So possible rational roots are:

$$
\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 6
$$

Let's test these values by plugging them into the polynomial.

- Try $ x = 1 $:
  $$
  1^3 - 6(1)^2 + 11(1) - 6 = 1 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 0 \quad \text{✓}
  $$
  So, **$ x = 1 $** is a root.

#### **Step 2: Polynomial Division**

Since $ x = 1 $ is a root, we can factor $ (x - 1) $ out of the polynomial.

We perform **polynomial long division** or **synthetic division**:

Using **synthetic division** with root 1:

```
1 |  1  -6  11  -6
    |     1  -5   6
  -------------------
      1  -5   6   0
```

So the quotient is:

$$
x^2 - 5x + 6
$$

Now we factor the quadratic:

$$
x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)
$$

#### **Step 3: Final Factorization**

$$
x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)
$$

#### ✅ **Roots:**
$$
x = 1, \quad x = 2, \quad x = 3
$$

---

3x - 4 \leq 2x + 5
$$

Subtract $ 2x $ from both sides:

$$
3x - 2x - 4 \leq 5
$$
$$
x - 4 \leq 5
$$

#### **Step 2: Add 4 to both sides**

$$
x \leq 9
$$

#### ✅ **Solution:**
$$
x \leq 9
$$

This means Amelia can safely travel through the Crystal Caverns when $ x $ is **less than or equal to 9**.

The largest planet in our solar system is undeniably Jupiter. Often referred to as a "gas giant," Jupiter dwarfs all other planets in terms of size and mass, presenting a truly awe-inspiring spectacle in the night sky. Its sheer scale is difficult to fully grasp, and even through powerful telescopes, its immense proportions remain a testament to the raw power of the universe. Understanding its size is the first step in appreciating the remarkable characteristics that make Jupiter such a unique and fascinating celestial body.

Jupiter’s diameter is approximately 140,000 kilometers (87,000 miles), which is more than eleven times the diameter of Earth. To put this into perspective, if the Sun were a basketball, Jupiter would be roughly the size of the United States – a truly vast expanse. This colossal size isn't just about length; Jupiter is also incredibly thick, possessing a substantial volume that holds an immense amount of hydrogen and helium, the primary elements that compose its atmosphere.

The planet’s mass is staggering, exceeding that of all the other planets in our solar system combined. Jupiter accounts for roughly 318 times the mass of Earth, making it the most massive planet by a significant margin. This immense mass creates an incredibly powerful gravitational field, which is responsible for the prominent and complex system of moons that orbit it.  It's this gravity that keeps these moons in stable orbits, creating a miniature solar system within Jupiter’s embrace.

One of Jupiter’s most striking features is the Great Red Spot, a persistent storm that has raged for at least 350 years – and possibly much longer. This enormous swirling vortex is larger than Earth itself and represents a level of atmospheric turbulence rarely seen elsewhere in the solar system. Scientists continue to study the Great Red Spot to better understand the dynamics of Jupiter’s atmosphere and the processes that drive these colossal storms.

Beyond the Great Red Spot, Jupiter’s atmosphere is a dynamic and turbulent mix of clouds composed of ammonia, water, and methane. These clouds create the planet’s iconic banded appearance, with alternating zones of lighter and darker hues. The colors are a result of the way sunlight interacts with these atmospheric compounds, producing a stunning visual display.

Jupiter’s internal structure is believed to consist of a small, dense core, surrounded by a vast layer of metallic hydrogen. This metallic hydrogen is under immense pressure, which allows it to conduct electricity and generate Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field – the strongest in the solar system. This magnetic field extends far beyond the planet, creating intense radiation belts that pose a significant hazard to spacecraft.

The planet’s moons are a captivating aspect of its character. Jupiter boasts a remarkable collection of over 95 known moons, each with its own unique features and characteristics. The four largest moons – Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto – are collectively known as the Galilean moons, discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610. These moons are incredibly diverse, ranging from Io, the most volcanically active body in the solar system, to Europa, which is believed to harbor a subsurface ocean.

In conclusion, Jupiter reigns supreme as the largest planet in our solar system, a colossal world of swirling storms, powerful gravity, and a captivating array of moons. Its sheer size, mass, and atmospheric complexity make it a subject of ongoing scientific investigation and a testament to the grandeur and diversity of our cosmic neighborhood.  It’s a planet that continues to inspire wonder and drive our understanding of planetary formation and evolution.

chosen.content: Implement a function `compute_lcm(num_list: List[int]) -> int` that accepts a list of integers and returns their least common multiple (LCM). The function should raise a ValueError if the list contains fewer than two integers or if any of the integers are not positive. You may assume that the list will not contain duplicate integers.

**Solution Overview**

The least‑common‑multiple (LCM) of two positive integers `a` and `b` can be computed with the well‑known formula  

\[
\text{lcm}(a,b)=\frac{a\;b}{\gcd(a,b)}
\]

where `gcd` is the greatest‑common‑divisor.  
Because the LCM operation is **associative** (`lcm(lcm(a,b),c) = lcm(a,b,c)`), we can obtain the LCM of an entire list by folding the pairwise operation over the list.

The implementation therefore follows three steps:

1. **Validate the input** – raise `ValueError` if the list has fewer than two elements or if any element is ≤ 0.
2. **Iteratively combine** the numbers using the pairwise LCM formula (leveraging `math.gcd` and `functools.reduce`).
3. **Return** the final result.

The function is fully typed, documented, and includes a small test‑suite that demonstrates the expected behaviour and the error handling.

---

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import math
import functools
from typing import List

def compute_lcm(num_list: List[int]) -> int:
    """
    Compute the least common multiple (LCM) of a list of positive integers.

    Parameters
    ----------
    num_list : List[int]
        A list containing **at least two** distinct positive integers.
        (Duplicates are not required to be handled specially – the caller
        guarantees they are absent.)

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The LCM of all numbers in ``num_list``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        * If ``num_list`` contains fewer than two elements.
        * If any element of ``num_list`` is not a positive integer.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> compute_lcm([4, 6])
    12
    >>> compute_lcm([3, 5, 7])
    105
    >>> compute_lcm([2, 3, 4, 5])
    60
    """
    # ---- 1️⃣ Input validation -------------------------------------------------
    if len(num_list) < 2:
        raise ValueError("At least two integers are required to compute an LCM.")

    for i, n in enumerate(num_list):
        if not isinstance(n, int):
            raise ValueError(f"Element at index {i} ({n!r}) is not an integer.")
        if n <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"Element at index {i} ({n}) is not a positive integer.")

    # ---- 2️⃣ Pairwise LCM helper -----------------------------------------------
    def lcm_pair(a: int, b: int) -> int:
        """Return lcm of two positive integers."""
        # math.gcd works with any sign, but we already know a,b > 0
        return a // math.gcd(a, b) * b   # avoid overflow by dividing first

    # ---- 3️⃣ Reduce the list ----------------------------------------------------
    return functools.reduce(lcm_pair, num_list)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Simple sanity‑check tests (run only when the module is executed directly) #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_cases = [
        ([4, 6], 12),
        ([3, 5, 7], 105),
        ([2, 3, 4, 5], 60),
        ([9, 12, 15], 180),
    ]

    for nums, expected in test_cases:
        result = compute_lcm(nums)
        assert result == expected, f"Failed for {nums}: got {result}, expected {expected}"
        print(f"LCM{tuple(nums)} = {result}")

    # Demonstrate error handling
    try:
        compute_lcm([42])                     # too few elements
    except ValueError as e:
        print("Correctly raised:", e)

    try:
        compute_lcm([5, -3, 7])                # negative number
    except ValueError as e:
        print("Correctly raised:", e)

    try:
        compute_lcm([2, 3.5])                  # non‑int
    except ValueError as e:
        print("Correctly raised:", e)
```

**Explanation of key points**

* **Validation** – The function checks both the *count* of numbers and the *sign* of each entry. It also guards against non‑integer types, providing a clear error message that includes the offending index.

* **Associativity** – Using `functools.reduce` cleanly folds the pairwise LCM across the whole list without extra loops.
* **Testing block** – When the script is run directly (`python compute_lcm.py`) it executes a few sanity checks and demonstrates the error cases, making it easy to verify correctness.

The function meets all the requirements: it returns the LCM for a valid list, raises `ValueError` for too‑short or non‑positive inputs, and assumes no duplicate values are present.

The factory offers a 70% discount and successfully sells 85% of the products. However, they have outstanding debts of $20000 to their suppliers. How much money will the factory have left after settling their debts?

We are given the following information:

- **Total products in stock**: 3000  
- **Original price per product**: $75  
- **Discount offered**: 70%  
- **Percentage of products sold**: 85%  
- **Outstanding debt to suppliers**: $20,000  

We need to calculate how much money the factory will have **left after selling the products and paying off the debt**.

---

### **Step 1: Calculate the number of products sold**

$$
\text{Products sold} = 3000 \times 0.85 = 2550
$$

---

### **Step 2: Calculate the discounted price per product**

A 70% discount means the product is sold at 30% of the original price:

$$
\text{Discounted price} = 75 \times (1 - 0.70) = 75 \times 0.30 = 22.50
$$

---

### **Step 3: Calculate total revenue from sales**

$$
\text{Total revenue} = 2550 \times 22.50 = 57,375
$$

---

### **Step 4: Subtract the debt**

$$
\text{Money left after paying debt} = 57,375 - 20,000 = 37,375
$$

---

### ✅ **Final Answer: $37,375**  
The factory will have **$37,375** left after settling their debts.

import sys

    if num < 2:
        return False
    for i in range(2, int(math.sqrt(num)) + 1):
        if num % i == 0:
            return False
    return True

def is_sophie_germain(p):

if __name__ == "__main__":

To solve this problem, we need to **understand the structure of the graph and the constraints imposed by flow conservation**.

---

## 🔍 Problem Summary

We are given a **directed graph** with a **flow-conservation constraint**:

> For every vertex `v`, the **sum of values on incoming edges** equals the **sum of values on outgoing edges**.

We are to find the **minimum number of edges** `E'` such that **knowing the values on those edges** allows us to **uniquely determine the values on all other edges** using the flow conservation law.

---

## 🧠 Key Observations

1. **Flow conservation** implies that the graph is a **flow network**, and the edge values must form a **circulation** (i.e., a flow with zero net flow at every node).

2. The problem is equivalent to finding the **minimum number of edges** to fix in a circulation such that the rest of the edge values can be uniquely determined.

3. This is a **graph-theoretic** problem. The solution is closely related to the **number of independent cycles** in the graph.

4. The number of **independent cycles** in a graph is given by the **cyclomatic number** or **circuit rank**:

   $$
   \text{Circuit Rank} = M - N + C
   $$

   where:
   - `M` is the number of edges
   - `N` is the number of vertices
   - `C` is the number of **weakly connected components** of the graph

   (In this problem, each component is **strongly connected**, so the weak and strong components are the same.)

5. In a **strongly connected component**, the **minimum number of edges** you must fix to determine the rest of the edge values is equal to the **circuit rank** of that component.

6. Therefore, the **minimum size of E'** is the **sum of the circuit ranks of all connected components**.

---

## ✅ Final Formula

For each test case:

- Compute the number of **connected components** `C`
- For each component:
  - Let `Mi` be the number of edges in component `i`
  - Let `Ni` be the number of vertices in component `i`
  - Then the contribution of component `i` to the answer is:  
    $$
    \text{rank}_i = M_i - N_i + 1
    $$
- The total answer is the **sum of all `rank_i`**

---

## 🧮 Implementation Steps

1. Parse the input.
2. For each test case:
   - Build the graph.
   - Use **DFS or BFS** to find the number of connected components and their sizes.
   - For each component, compute `M_i - N_i + 1`.
   - Sum these values to get the answer.

---

## 🧪 Example

### Sample Input 3:

```
4 4
1 2
2 1
3 4
4 3
```

- 2 components:
  - Component 1: {1, 2}, 2 edges → rank = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1
  - Component 2: {3, 4}, 2 edges → rank = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1
- Total = 1 + 1 = **2**

✅ Matches the sample output.

---

## 🧑‍💻 Python Code

```python
import sys
from collections import defaultdict, deque

sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def main():
    input = sys.stdin.read
    data = input().split()
    
    idx = 0
    while idx < len(data):
        N = int(data[idx])
        M = int(data[idx+1])
        idx += 2
        
        edges = []
        for _ in range(M):
            u = int(data[idx]) - 1
            v = int(data[idx+1]) - 1
            edges.append((u, v))
            idx += 2
        
        # Build adjacency list
        graph = defaultdict(list)
        for u, v in edges:
            graph[u].append(v)
        
        visited = [False] * N
        total_rank = 0

        for i in range(N):
            if not visited[i]:
                # BFS to find component
                queue = deque()
                queue.append(i)
                visited[i] = True
                component_nodes = 0
                component_edges = 0
                component = set()
                component.add(i)

                while queue:
                    u = queue.popleft()
                    component_nodes += 1
                    for v in graph[u]:
                        if v not in component:
                            component.add(v)
                            visited[v] = True
                            queue.append(v)
                        component_edges += 1  # Count all edges in the component

                # Each edge is counted once per source
                # So we must divide by 2 if we double-counted
                # But since we're building the adjacency list as a directed graph,
                # and we're counting all edges from each node, we have counted each edge once.
                # So component_edges is the correct count.

                # Compute circuit rank for this component
                rank = component_edges - component_nodes + 1
                total_rank += rank

        print(total_rank)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

---

## ✅ Time Complexity

- For each test case:
  - `O(M + N)` for BFS
  - Efficient for `N ≤ 500`, `M ≤ 3000`

---

- The problem is essentially about **determining the number of independent cycles** in each component.
- Each cycle gives **one degree of freedom**, so we must fix **one edge per cycle** to determine the rest.
- This is why the answer is the **sum of the circuit ranks** of all components.

On any spacetime $(M,g)$ we can form the causal ordering $\leq$, where for any two points $a,b \in M$ we have that $a \leq b$ iff there exists some future directed, non-spacelike curve from $a$ to $b$. This causal ordering is transitive, irreflexive, antisymmetry and dense in general. However, causal oddities like CTC's manifest as violations of irreflexivity and antisymmetry.
I'm interested in the directedness of the causal order (unfortunate name, I know). Recall that a relation $\leq$ is directed iff for any two elements $a,b \in M$ there is some third element $c \in M$ such that both $a \leq c$ and $b \leq c$. 
I can see that a Minkowksi space has a directed causal order. I have no proof, but the picture below is good enough to convince me. I have heard that for non-flat spacetimes, directedness of the causal order is not guaranteed. Are there any concrete examples of this? And, moreover, is there some appropriate causality condition one can impose on the spacetime in order to guarantee directedness of the causal order?

You've hit on a very interesting and subtle point in causal structure! You're right to be suspicious about directedness not holding in general, and you're correct that it's related to causal oddities. Let's break down the issue, provide examples, and discuss conditions for directedness.

**Why Directedness Can Fail**

The intuition you have for Minkowski space is excellent.  The 'shaded area' represents the region of future-directed timelike/null paths, providing a witness `c` for the directedness condition.  The problem arises when the spacetime doesn't have enough 'room' in its causal future to allow such a witness to exist *for all* pairs of points.  This is most readily seen when causal curves "get stuck" or when the causal future of a point is limited.

**Concrete Examples of Non-Directed Causal Orders**

1. **Gödel Spacetime:** This is the classic example. Gödel spacetime is a solution to Einstein's field equations featuring a rotating universe. It *contains closed timelike curves (CTCs)*.  Because of the CTCs, the causal order is not irreflexive (a point can be causally related to itself via a CTC).  Crucially, Gödel spacetime is *not* directed.  You can find points *a* and *b* such that there is no *c* satisfying *a* ≤ *c* and *b* ≤ *c*.  The rotation prevents the causal futures from "meeting" in a way that guarantees a witness.

2. **Spacetimes with "Trapped Surfaces" and Limited Causal Futures:** Consider a spacetime where points are "trapped" within a region where all future-directed paths eventually lead back towards the starting point (like a very strong gravitational well).  If two points are on opposite sides of this "trap", it might be impossible to find a point *c* that both can causally reach.  This isn't necessarily a CTC situation, but it demonstrates how a restricted causal future can break directedness.

3. **Spacetimes with a "Boundary" to Causal Influence:**  Imagine a spacetime where there's a region that causally isolates other regions.  If *a* and *b* are in different isolated regions, there might be no point *c* that can be reached from both.

4. **More Exotic Examples:** There are even more contrived examples built specifically to violate directedness, often involving carefully constructed topological features.  These are often used in mathematical relativity to explore the limits of causal structure.

**Causality Conditions Guaranteeing Directedness**

The key is to impose conditions that prevent the causal structure from being "too restricted" or "too looped." Here are some relevant conditions:

1. **Global Hyperbolicity:** This is a strong condition that guarantees a well-behaved causal structure. A spacetime is globally hyperbolic if it admits a smooth, globally hyperbolic maximal Cauchy surface.  *Globally hyperbolic spacetimes are always directed.*  This is a powerful result.  Global hyperbolicity essentially means that the spacetime has a "time function" and that causal curves don't loop back on themselves in a problematic way.  It's a very common assumption in mathematical relativity.

2. **Causal Simplicity:** A spacetime is causally simple if it has no closed causal curves and the causal future of any point is open.  *Causal simplicity implies directedness.* The openness of the causal future is crucial; it prevents the "getting stuck" scenarios.

3. **Existence of a Timelike Boundary:**  If a spacetime has a timelike boundary, and the causal structure is "well-behaved" near the boundary, directedness can be guaranteed.  (The precise conditions depend on the nature of the boundary.)

4. **Strongly Causal Spacetimes:** A spacetime is strongly causal if for any two points *a* and *b*, if *a* and *b* are causally related, then there is a unique causal curve connecting them.  While not *sufficient* for directedness, it's a strong condition that often accompanies other properties that *do* guarantee directedness.

**Relationship to Other Causality Conditions**

* **Causality:**  A spacetime is causal if it has no closed timelike curves.  Causality is *not* sufficient for directedness (Gödel spacetime is causal but not directed).
* **Lorentzian Geodesic Completeness:** This means that every timelike and null geodesic can be extended indefinitely.  This is often assumed in general relativity, but it doesn't guarantee directedness on its own.

**In Summary**

Directedness of the causal order is a stronger property than just having a well-defined causal order (i.e., no CTCs).  It requires that the causal structure is "rich enough" to allow for a witness point *c* for any pair of points *a* and *b*.  Spacetimes like Gödel spacetime demonstrate that this isn't always the case.  Strong causality conditions like global hyperbolicity or causal simplicity are needed to guarantee directedness.

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n == 2:
        return True
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return False
    for i in range(3, int(n**0.5) + 1, 2):
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
    return True

def is_palindrome(n):
    return str(n) == str(n)[::-1]

For example, it can be a crime to drive without licence, to sell stable food, to pollute a river, to interfere with a witness in a lawsuit or to bribe an official.
The rationale for eliminating the mens rea requirement in such offences is that to require the prosecution to establish the defendant's intent, or even recklessness, would render such regulatory legislation largely ineffective and unenforceable. Such cases are known in Anglo-American law as strict liability offences. In German law they are excluded because the requirement of mens rea is considered a constitutional principle.
There has been considerable criticism of statutes that create liability without actual moral fault. To expose citizens to the condemnation of a criminal conviction without a showing of moral culpability raises issues of justice. In many instances, the objectives of such legislation can more effectively be achieved by civil sanctions, such as suits for damages and the revocation of licences.

To predict the **number of possible bombs** in a **5x5 Minesweeper board** based on the **user input** of how many **safe spots** they have selected, we can use a **statistical approach**.

---

### 🎯 Objective:

Given:
- A **5x5 board** (25 total cells)
- The user selects **N safe spots** (N ≤ 10)
- The **number of bombs** is to be predicted
- We have **past game data** (a list of numbers representing bomb positions or patterns)

We will:
1. Use the **historical data** to find the **distribution of bombs** in the 25-cell board.
2. Use this to **predict** the number of bombs for the **next game**, given **N safe spots**.

---

## ✅ Step-by-step Plan:

### 1. **Preprocess the Data**
We are given a raw list of numbers. Let's assume each number in the list is a **cell index** (1 to 25) where a bomb was located in previous games.

We will count how many times each cell was a bomb in the past.

---

### 2. **Create Bomb Probability Map**
We count how many times each cell was a bomb in the past, and then compute the **probability** of each cell being a bomb.

---

### 3. **Simulate Game**
Given **N safe spots**, we remove those from the 25 cells, and use the **remaining 25 - N** cells to **predict the number of bombs** using the **probability distribution**.

---

### 4. **Predict Bomb Count**
Using the probability map, we simulate the expected number of bombs in the **remaining cells**.

---

## ✅ Python Code

```python
import numpy as np

# --- Step 1: Raw data of bomb positions in past games
past_bomb_positions = [
    8, 11, 21, 4, 10, 15, 12, 17, 18, 6, 8, 23, 9, 10, 14, 1, 12, 21, 9, 17,
    19, 1, 2, 23, 6, 13, 14, 16, 21, 24, 6, 15, 20, 2, 12, 13, 9, 11, 14, 1, 10,
    11, 20, 22, 24, 1, 14, 20, 1, 21, 23, 4, 8, 24, 3, 10, 11, 5, 17, 23, 1, 13,

    18, 3, 7, 17, 7, 15, 18, 4, 7, 21, 6, 7, 23, 2, 19, 23, 1, 14, 15, 3, 21, 23,
    4, 9, 10, 5, 6, 12, 2, 18, 24, 3, 11, 13, 8, 14, 23, 14, 21, 23, 5, 8, 13,
    11, 12, 19, 2, 10, 19, 2, 18, 23, 2, 4, 5, 12, 15
]

# --- Step 2: Count bomb occurrences for each cell (1 to 25)
bomb_counts = [0] * 25  # 0-indexed cells from 0 to 24
for pos in past_bomb_positions:
    index = pos - 1  # convert 1-based to 0-based
    bomb_counts[index] += 1

# --- Step 3: Compute probability of each cell being a bomb
total_games = len(past_bomb_positions)
probabilities = [count / total_games for count in bomb_counts]

# --- Step 4: User input
def predict_bombs(safe_spots):
    safe_spots = [int(s) - 1 for s in safe_spots]  # Convert to 0-based
    available_cells = [i for i in range(25) if i not in safe_spots]
    
    expected_bombs = sum(probabilities[i] for i in available_cells)
    return round(expected_bombs)

# --- Step 5: Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example input from user
    user_safe_spots = input("Enter the safe spots (comma-separated, max 10, 1-25): ").strip()
    safe_spots = [int(x) for x in user_safe_spots.split(",")]

    elif any(not (1 <= s <= 25) for s in safe_spots):
        print("Error: Safe spots must be between 1 and 25.")
    else:
        predicted_bombs = predict_bombs(safe_spots)
        print(f"Predicted number of bombs: {predicted_bombs}")

chosen.content: Can you detail what cyberstalking means?

Cyberstalking is a form of online harassment and intimidation that involves the use of digital technology to stalk, monitor, or harass an individual. It is a modern form of stalking that occurs through the internet, social media, email, messaging apps, and other online platforms.

### Key Characteristics of Cyberstalking:

1. **Digital Monitoring:**
   - Tracking someone's online activity, such as browsing history, location, or social media posts.
   - Using tools like IP geolocation, screen recording, or spyware to monitor a person's online behavior.

2. **Threats and Intimidation:**
   - Sending threatening messages, emails, or messages online.
   - Using social media to post harmful or embarrassing content about the person.
   - Sending unwanted messages or calls, often with a sense of urgency or fear.

3. **Online Harassment:**
   - Posting derogatory or offensive comments, photos, or videos online.
   - Using fake profiles or impersonating the person to harass them.

4. **Persistent and Unwanted Contact:**
   - Repeatedly contacting the person through various online channels.
   - Using social media to spread rumors or false information about the person.

5. **Psychological Impact:**
   - Causing anxiety, fear, or distress.
   - Making the person feel unsafe or vulnerable online.

### Common Forms of Cyberstalking:

- **Online Harassment:** Posting derogatory or threatening content online.
- **Social Media Stalking:** Following, commenting on, or sharing content about someone without their consent.
- **Phishing and Scams:** Using email or social media to trick someone into revealing personal information.
- **Cyberbullying:** Using the internet to harass, intimidate, or humiliate someone.
- **Spam and Spamming:** Sending unsolicited messages or emails to the person.
- **Spyware and Tracking:** Installing software to monitor online activity.

### Legal and Ethical Considerations:

- **Legal Protection:** In many countries, cyberstalking is illegal and can result in legal consequences, including fines or imprisonment.
- **Privacy Rights:** Individuals have the right to privacy and protection from unwanted online surveillance.
- **Ethical Responsibility:** Online platforms and users have a responsibility to respect others' privacy and avoid harassment.

### How to Protect Yourself from Cyberstalking:

- **Use Strong Passwords and Two-Factor Authentication.**
- **Be Cautious with Personal Information.**
- **Report Unwanted Activity to the Platform.**
- **Seek Support from Friends, Family, or Professionals.**
- **Consult a Lawyer or Cybersecurity Expert.**

### Conclusion:

Cyberstalking is a serious issue in the digital age, affecting individuals' mental and emotional well-being. It is important to recognize the signs of cyberstalking and take steps to protect oneself online. If you or someone you know is being cyberstalked, it is important to seek help and take legal action when necessary.

chosen.content: A bakery sells 240 cupcakes in April, 260 in May, and a certain number of cupcakes in June. If the average number of cupcakes sold per month across all three months is 270, how many cupcakes did the bakery sell in June?

We are given:

- April: 240 cupcakes  
- May: 260 cupcakes  
- June: ? cupcakes  
- Average number of cupcakes sold per month over 3 months = 270

---

### Step 1: Use the formula for average

$$
\text{Average} = \frac{\text{Total cupcakes sold over 3 months}}{3}
$$

We are told the average is 270, so:

$$
270 = \frac{240 + 260 + x}{3}
$$

Where $ x $ is the number of cupcakes sold in June.

---

### Step 2: Multiply both sides by 3

$$
270 \times 3 = 240 + 260 + x
$$

$$
810 = 500 + x
$$

---

### Step 3: Solve for $ x $

$$
x = 810 - 500 = 310
$$

---

### ✅ Final Answer:

$$
\boxed{310}
$$

The bakery sold **310 cupcakes in June**.

\[
240 + 260 + x = 810 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 810 - 500 = 310.
\]

As an information technology (IT) specialist, you often encounter network systems represented by complex graphs. Each node in the graph represents a server, and each edge represents a communication link between two servers. Your task is to ensure efficient data transfer across the network.

1. Consider a network represented by a weighted, undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) where the weights on the edges signify the bandwidth of the communication link between two servers (nodes). You need to determine the maximum bandwidth path between two servers \(A\) and \(B\). Formulate the problem of finding this path as an optimization problem and provide the mathematical representation.

2. Given that the network graph \(G\) might be subject to failures, each edge has a reliability factor \(r(e)\) associated with it, where \(0 \leq r(e) \leq 1\). The reliability of a path is the product of the reliabilities of its edges. Determine the path between servers \(A\) and \(B\) that maximizes the reliability. Provide the mathematical formulation and explain how you would approach solving this problem.

**1.  Maximum‑bandwidth (bottleneck) path**

Let  

* \(G=(V,E)\) be a weighted, undirected graph.  
* \(w(e)\;(e\in E)\) be the bandwidth of link \(e\).  
* \(A,B\in V\) be the two servers between which we want the most‑bandwidth path.  

The *bandwidth* of a path \(P\subseteq E\) is the smallest bandwidth among the links that belong to the path (the “bottleneck” edge).  
We therefore want

\[
\max_{P\subseteq E\ \text{connects }A\text{ to }B}\;\min_{e\in P} w(e).
\]

---

### Integer‑programming formulation

Introduce a binary variable for every edge

\[
x_e=\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if edge }e\text{ is used in the path},\\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\qquad e\in E.
\]

Introduce a continuous variable \(t\) that will represent the bandwidth of the chosen path.  
The following constraints guarantee that the selected edges form a simple path from \(A\) to \(B\) and that \(t\) is the minimum bandwidth on that path.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(x_e\) | edge‑selection binary variable |
| \(t\)   | bandwidth of the chosen path |

**Objective**

\[
\max\; t
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Flow conservation (path structure)**  

   For every vertex \(v\in V\):

   \[
   \sum_{e\in\delta(v)} x_e = 
   \begin{cases}
   1 & \text{if } v=A\text{ or }v=B,\\[4pt]
   2 & \text{otherwise},
   \end{cases}
   \]
   where \(\delta(v)\) is the set of edges incident to \(v\).  
   (Every internal vertex has degree 2 on the path, the two end vertices have degree 1.)

2. **Bottleneck link**  

   For every edge \(e\in E\):

   \[
   t \;\le\; w(e)\,x_e .
   \]

   If \(x_e=0\) the inequality is vacuous; if \(x_e=1\) it forces \(t\le w(e)\).  
   Hence \(t\) cannot exceed the bandwidth of any edge that is part of the path.

3. **Binary / continuous domains**

   \[
   x_e\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall e\in E,\qquad t\ge 0.
   \]

This is a classic *max‑min* (bottleneck) path problem.  
Because the objective is linear and all constraints are linear, the problem can be solved with any MILP solver.  
If the graph is large, one may also use the **maximum‑capacity path algorithm** (a variant of Dijkstra that propagates the minimum edge weight along the path) which runs in \(O(|E|+|V|\log|V|)\) time.

---

**2.  Maximum‑reliability path**

Each edge \(e\) has a reliability factor \(r(e)\in[0,1]\).  
The reliability of a path \(P\) is the product of the reliabilities of its edges:

\[
\operatorname{Rel}(P)=\prod_{e\in P} r(e).
\]

We want

\[
\max_{P\subseteq E\ \text{connects }A\text{ to }B}\;\prod_{e\in P} r(e).
\]

---

### Mathematical formulation

Because the product is multiplicative, it is convenient to take logarithms.  
Let \(\ell(e)=\log r(e)\) (note that \(\ell(e)\le 0\)).  
Then

\[
\log\operatorname{Rel}(P)=\sum_{e\in P}\ell(e).
\]

Thus maximizing the product is equivalent to maximizing the sum of \(\ell(e)\) (or, equivalently, minimizing the sum of \(-\ell(e)\)).  

Using the same edge‑selection variables \(x_e\) as above, we obtain

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(x_e\) | edge‑selection binary variable |
| \(t\)   | (optional) reliability of the chosen path (not needed in the log‑formulation) |

**Objective**

\[
\max\; \sum_{e\in E} \ell(e)\,x_e
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\min\; \sum_{e\in E} (-\ell(e))\,x_e .
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Path structure** – the same flow‑conservation constraints as in part 1:

   \[
   \sum_{e\in\delta(v)} x_e = 
   \begin{cases}
   1 & \text{if } v=A\text{ or }v=B,\\[4pt]
   2 & \text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
   \]

2. **Domains**

   \[
   x_e\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall e\in E.
   \]

This is a **0–1 linear program**.  
Because the objective coefficients \(-\ell(e)=-\log r(e)\) are non‑negative (every \(r(e)\le1\)), the problem is equivalent to a *shortest‑path* problem with edge costs \(c(e)=-\log r(e)\).  

---

### Solving the problem

1. **Shortest‑path approach**  
   * Compute \(c(e)=-\log r(e)\) for every edge.  
   * Run Dijkstra’s algorithm (or any shortest‑path algorithm) from \(A\) to \(B\).  
   * The resulting path minimises \(\sum c(e)\) and therefore maximises \(\prod r(e)\).  
   * Complexity: \(O(|E|+|V|\log|V|)\).

2. **MILP approach**  
   * If you need to add extra constraints (e.g., a limit on the number of hops, or a requirement that the path must avoid certain nodes), keep the integer‑program formulation above and solve with an MILP solver.  
   * For large networks, the shortest‑path reduction is usually preferable because it is linear‑time in practice.

---

**Summary**

| Problem | Objective | Key formulation | Typical algorithm |
|---------|-----------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Max‑bandwidth (bottleneck) | \(\max \min_{e\in P} w(e)\) | MILP with variable \(t\) and constraints \(t\le w(e)x_e\) | Dijkstra‑style maximum‑capacity path |
| Max‑reliability | \(\max \prod_{e\in P} r(e)\) | MILP with objective \(\sum \log r(e)\,x_e\) (or shortest‑path with costs \(-\log r(e)\)) | Dijkstra on transformed weights |

Both problems can be expressed as integer programs, but in practice the bandwidth problem is solved by a specialized maximum‑capacity algorithm, while the reliability problem reduces to a standard shortest‑path problem after a logarithmic transformation.

2. Given that the network graph \(G\) might be subject to failures, each edge has a reliability factor \(r(e)\) associated with it, where \(0 \leq r(e) \leq 1\). The reliability of a path is the product of the reliabilities of its edges. Determine the path between servers \(A\) and \(B\) that maximizes the reliability. To address the given problem, we need to tackle two distinct optimization problems: finding the maximum bandwidth path and then the path with maximum reliability under edge failures.

### Part 1: Maximum Bandwidth Path

1. **Formulation as an Optimization Problem:**

   We are given a weighted, undirected graph \( G = (V, E) \) where each edge \( e \in E \) has a weight \( w(e) \) representing the bandwidth. The goal is to find a path from node \( A \) to node \( B \) that maximizes the total bandwidth.

   Let \( P \) be a path from \( A \) to \( B \) in the graph. The objective is to maximize the sum of the weights of the edges in this path:

   \[
   \text{Maximize } \sum_{e \in P} w(e)
   \]

   **Constraints:**

   - The path \( P \) must start at node \( A \).
   - The path \( P \) must end at node \( B \).
   - Each edge \( e \in P \) can be included in the path, and its weight \( w(e) \) is non-negative.

   This is a classic shortest path problem with additional constraints on edge weights, which can be solved using various optimization techniques like Dijkstra's algorithm adapted for weighted graphs or Bellman-Ford algorithm for graphs with negative weights.

   **Mathematical Representation:**

   \[
   \text{Maximize } \sum_{e \in \text{path } P} w(e)
   \]

   Subject to:
   - \( \text{start}(P) = A \)
   - \( \text{end}(P) = B \)
   - \( w(e) \geq 0 \) for all \( e \in P \)

### Part 2: Maximum Reliability Path

2. **Reliability of a Path:**

   Each edge \( e \) has a reliability \( r(e) \). The reliability of a path \( P \) is the product of the reliabilities of its edges:

   \[
   \text{Reliability}(P) = \prod_{e \in P} r(e)
   \]

   **Formulation as an Optimization Problem:**

   We need to find a path \( P \) from \( A \) to \( B \) that maximizes the reliability:

   \[
   \text{Maximize } \text{Reliability}(P) = \prod_{e \in P} r(e)
   \]

   **Approach to Solve:**

   - **Dynamic Programming Approach:** Use a dynamic programming table where each cell \( dp[i][j] \) represents the maximum reliability of a path ending at node \( i \) with the first edge selected from the set of edges from \( A \) to \( j \).

     \]
     \[
     dp[i][j] = 0 \quad \text{for } i > 0, j > 0
     \]

     Fill the table iteratively:
     \[
     dp[i][j] = \max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1] \cdot r(e))
     \]
     for each edge \( e \) from \( A \) to \( j \).

   - **Solution:**

     The answer will be found in \( dp[B][B] \).

   **Conclusion:**

   The path \( P \) with the maximum reliability is the one for which the final entry in the \( dp \) table is maximized.

\[
\boxed{\text{dp[B][B]}}
\] 

This solution leverages dynamic programming to efficiently compute the maximum reliability path, considering both the direct path and all possible edge choices.

Each department has a different patient flow rate, which is represented by a continuous function \( f_i(t) \), where \( i \) is the department index and \( t \) is the time in days. The patient flow functions are defined as follows: 

1. Cardiology: \( f_1(t) = 30 + 10\sin(0.5t) \)
2. Neurology: \( f_2(t) = 20 + 8\cos(0.3t) \)
3. Oncology: \( f_3(t) = 25 + 12\sin(0.4t) \)
4. Pediatrics: \( f_4(t) = 18 + 5\cos(0.6t) \)
5. Orthopedics: \( f_5(t) = 22 + 7\sin(0.2t) \)

The analyst needs to solve the following problems:

1. Determine the total patient flow over a 30-day period for each department, and identify which department has the highest average patient flow over this period.

2. Assuming the hospital can allocate a maximum of 400 resource units per day across all departments, formulate a strategy to allocate resources such that each department receives a proportional share based on its average patient flow. Provide a mathematical expression for the resource allocation function for each department over the 30-day period.

We are given five departments with time-dependent patient flow functions $ f_i(t) $, and we are to:

1. Compute the **total patient flow over 30 days** for each department and determine which has the **highest average patient flow**.
2. Allocate **a maximum of 400 resource units per day** across departments **proportionally to their average patient flow**, and provide a **mathematical expression** for the daily resource allocation per department.

---

### **Step 1: Total Patient Flow Over 30 Days**

The total patient flow for department $ i $ over 30 days is the integral of $ f_i(t) $ from $ t = 0 $ to $ t = 30 $:

$$
\text{Total}_i = \int_0^{30} f_i(t) \, dt
$$

The **average patient flow** over 30 days is:

$$
\text{Average}_i = \frac{1}{30} \int_0^{30} f_i(t) \, dt = \frac{\text{Total}_i}{30}
$$

Let’s compute each one.

---

#### **1. Cardiology**: $ f_1(t) = 30 + 10\sin(0.5t) $

$$
\text{Total}_1 = \int_0^{30} \left(30 + 10\sin(0.5t)\right) dt = \int_0^{30} 30 \, dt + 10 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.5t) \, dt
$$

- $ \int_0^{30} 30 \, dt = 30 \times 30 = 900 $
- $ \int \sin(0.5t) \, dt = -\frac{1}{0.5} \cos(0.5t) = -2\cos(0.5t) $

So:

$$
10 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.5t) \, dt = 10 \left[ -2\cos(0.5t) \right]_0^{30} = 10 \left( -2\cos(15) + 2\cos(0) \right) = 20 \left(1 - \cos(15)\right)
$$

Note: $ \cos(15) $ is in **radians**. $ 15 $ radians ≈ $ 15 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 859.4^\circ $, so we compute:

$$
\cos(15) \approx \cos(15 \mod 2\pi) \approx \cos(15 - 4\pi) \quad \text{(since } 4\pi \approx 12.566\text{)}
$$
$ 15 - 12.566 = 2.434 $ radians

$ \cos(2.434) \approx \cos(139.5^\circ) \approx -0.760 $

So:

$$
20(1 - (-0.760)) = 20(1.760) = 35.2
$$

Thus:

$$
\text{Total}_1 = 900 + 35.2 = 935.2
$$

$$
\text{Average}_1 = \frac{935.2}{30} \approx 31.173
$$

---

#### **2. Neurology**: $ f_2(t) = 20 + 8\cos(0.3t) $

$$
\text{Total}_2 = \int_0^{30} \left(20 + 8\cos(0.3t)\right) dt = 20 \times 30 + 8 \int_0^{30} \cos(0.3t) \, dt
$$

- $ 20 \times 30 = 600 $
- $ \int \cos(0.3t) \, dt = \frac{1}{0.3} \sin(0.3t) = \frac{10}{3} \sin(0.3t) $

So:

$$
8 \int_0^{30} \cos(0.3t) \, dt = 8 \cdot \frac{10}{3} \left[ \sin(0.3t) \right]_0^{30} = \frac{80}{3} \left( \sin(9) - \sin(0) \right) = \frac{80}{3} \sin(9)
$$

$ 9 $ radians ≈ $ 9 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 515.7^\circ $, $ 515.7 - 360 = 155.7^\circ $

$ \sin(9) \approx \sin(155.7^\circ) = \sin(180^\circ - 24.3^\circ) = \sin(24.3^\circ) \approx 0.411 $

So:

$$
\frac{80}{3} \times 0.411 \approx 26.666 \times 0.411 \approx 10.96
$$

$$
\text{Total}_2 = 600 + 10.96 = 610.96
$$

$$
\text{Average}_2 = \frac{610.96}{30} \approx 20.365
$$

---

#### **3. Oncology**: $ f_3(t) = 25 + 12\sin(0.4t) $

$$
\text{Total}_3 = \int_0^{30} \left(25 + 12\sin(0.4t)\right) dt = 25 \times 30 + 12 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.4t) \, dt
$$

- $ 750 $
- $ \int \sin(0.4t) \, dt = -\frac{1}{0.4} \cos(0.4t) = -2.5 \cos(0.4t) $

So:

$$
12 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.4t) \, dt = 12 \left[ -2.5 \cos(0.4t) \right]_0^{30} = -30 \left( \cos(12) - \cos(0) \right) = -30 (\cos(12) - 1)
$$

$ 12 $ radians ≈ $ 12 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 687.5^\circ $, $ 687.5 - 360 = 327.5^\circ $, $ \cos(327.5^\circ) = \cos(-32.5^\circ) = \cos(32.5^\circ) \approx 0.843 $

So:

$$
-30 (0.843 - 1) = -30 (-0.157) = 4.71
$$

$$
\text{Total}_3 = 750 + 4.71 = 754.71
$$

$$
\text{Average}_3 = \frac{754.71}{30} \approx 25.157
$$

---

#### **4. Pediatrics**: $ f_4(t) = 18 + 5\cos(0.6t) $

$$
\text{Total}_4 = \int_0^{30} \left(18 + 5\cos(0.6t)\right) dt = 18 \times 30 + 5 \int_0^{30} \cos(0.6t) \, dt
$$

- $ 540 $
- $ \int \cos(0.6t) \, dt = \frac{1}{0.6} \sin(0.6t) = \frac{5}{3} \sin(0.6t) $

So:

$$
5 \int_0^{30} \cos(0.6t) \, dt = 5 \cdot \frac{5}{3} \left[ \sin(0.6t) \right]_0^{30} = \frac{25}{3} \left( \sin(18) - \sin(0) \right) = \frac{25}{3} \sin(18)
$$

$ 18 $ radians ≈ $ 18 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 1031.3^\circ $, $ 1031.3 - 2 \times 360 = 311.3^\circ $, $ \sin(311.3^\circ) = -\sin(48.7^\circ) \approx -0.751 $

So:

$$
\frac{25}{3} \times (-0.751) \approx 8.333 \times (-0.751) \approx -6.26
$$

$$
\text{Total}_4 = 540 - 6.26 = 533.74
$$

$$
\text{Average}_4 = \frac{533.74}{30} \approx 17.791
$$

---

#### **5. Orthopedics**: $ f_5(t) = 22 + 7\sin(0.2t) $

$$
\text{Total}_5 = \int_0^{30} \left(22 + 7\sin(0.2t)\right) dt = 22 \times 30 + 7 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.2t) \, dt
$$

- $ 660 $
- $ \int \sin(0.2t) \, dt = -\frac{1}{0.2} \cos(0.2t) = -5 \cos(0.2t) $

So:

$$
7 \int_0^{30} \sin(0.2t) \, dt = 7 \left[ -5 \cos(0.2t) \right]_0^{30} = -35 \left( \cos(6) - \cos(0) \right) = -35 (\cos(6) - 1)
$$

$ 6 $ radians ≈ $ 343.8^\circ $, $ \cos(6) = \cos(343.8^\circ) = \cos(-16.2^\circ) \approx 0.960 $

So:

$$
-35 (0.960 - 1) = -35 (-0.04) = 1.4
$$

$$
\text{Total}_5 = 660 + 1.4 = 661.4
$$

$$
\text{Average}_5 = \frac{661.4}{30} \approx 22.047
$$

---

### **Summary of Averages (over 30 days):**

| Department    | Total Flow | Average Flow |
|---------------|------------|--------------|
| Cardiology    | 935.2      | **31.173**   |
| Neurology     | 610.96     | 20.365       |
| Oncology      | 754.71     | 25.157       |
| Pediatrics    | 533.74     | 17.791       |
| Orthopedics   | 661.4      | 22.047       |

✅ **Cardiology has the highest average patient flow: ~31.173 patients/day**

---

### **Step 2: Proportional Resource Allocation**

The hospital can allocate **at most 400 resource units per day**.

We want to allocate resources **proportionally to the average patient flow**.

Let:

- $ A_i $ = average patient flow for department $ i $
- $ A_{\text{total}} = \sum_{i=1}^5 A_i $

Then, the **daily resource allocation** for department $ i $ is:

$$
R_i(t) = 400 \times \frac{A_i}{A_{\text{total}}}
$$

Note: Since the allocation is based on **average flow**, and we are allocating **per day**, the allocation is **constant over time** (i.e., not time-varying), but proportional to the average patient volume.

---

#### **Compute Total Average Flow:**

$$
A_{\text{total}} = 31.173 + 20.365 + 25.157 + 17.791 + 22.047 = 
$$

Let’s add:

- 31.173 + 20.365 = 51.538
- +25.157 = 76.695
- +17.791 = 94.486
- +22.047 = **116.533**

So:

$$
A_{\text{total}} \approx 116.533
$$

---

#### **Resource Allocation per Department (Daily):**

$$
R_i = 400 \times \frac{A_i}{116.533}
$$

Now compute each:

1. **Cardiology**:
   $$
   R_1 = 400 \times \frac{31.173}{116.533} \approx 400 \times 0.2675 \approx 107.00
   $$

2. **Neurology**:
   $$
   R_2 = 400 \times \frac{20.365}{116.533} \approx 400 \times 0.1747 \approx 69.88
   $$

3. **Oncology**:
   $$
   R_3 = 400 \times \frac{25.157}{116.533} \approx 400 \times 0.2159 \approx 86.36
   $$

4. **Pediatrics**:
   $$
   R_4 = 400 \times \frac{17.791}{116.533} \approx 400 \times 0.1527 \approx 61.08
   $$

5. **Orthopedics**:
   $$
   R_5 = 400 \times \frac{22.047}{116.533} \approx 400 \times 0.1892 \approx 75.68
   $$

Let’s check sum:

$$
107.00 + 69.88 + 86.36 + 61.08 + 75.68 = 400.00 \quad \text{✓}
$$

---

### ✅ **Final Answers:**

---

### **1. Total and Average Patient Flow (30-day period):**

| Department    | Total Flow | Average Flow |
|---------------|------------|--------------|
| Cardiology    | 935.2      | **31.173**   |
| Neurology     | 610.96     | 20.365       |
| Oncology      | 754.71     | 25.157       |
| Pediatrics    | 533.74     | 17.791       |
| Orthopedics   | 661.4      | 22.047       |

✅ **Cardiology has the highest average patient flow.**

---

### **2. Resource Allocation Strategy:**

The hospital should allocate **400 resource units per day**, distributed **proportionally to the average patient flow**.

The **daily resource allocation function** for each department is **constant** (independent of time $ t $) and given by:

$$
R_i(t) = 400 \times \frac{A_i}{\sum_{j=1}^5 A_j} = 400 \times \frac{A_i}{116.533}
$$

Where $ A_i $ is the average patient flow for department $ i $.

Explicitly:

- **Cardiology**: $ R_1(t) = 107.00 $
- **Neurology**: $ R_2(t) = 69.88 $
- **Oncology**: $ R_3(t) = 86.36 $
- **Pediatrics**: $ R_4(t) = 61.08 $
- **Orthopedics**: $ R_5(t) = 75.68 $

> ✅ **These allocations are constant over time and sum to 400 units per day.**

---

### ✅ **Conclusion:**

- **Cardiology** is the busiest department on average.
- The optimal resource allocation strategy is **proportional to average patient flow**, resulting in **fixed daily allocations** as above.

This ensures resources are distributed fairly and efficiently based on patient demand.
